rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Night Journey probably occurred a year or two before the Hijrah; most Companions held that it was physical, while a few understood it as purely spiritual.
rows.anchor: considered by most to have taken place a year or two prior to the migration to Madinah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tradition describes Gabriel taking Muhammad on Burāq to Jerusalem and through seven heavens to God in a single night, outside ordinary time; one report says his door still swung on return.
rows.anchor: The Prophet was reportedly taken upon a winged horse, named Burāq, and led by the Archangel Gabriel to Jerusalem

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mainstream tradition regards the Ascension as both bodily and spiritual and a special prophetic miracle; some Muslims, especially Sufis, see spiritual ascension as possible through a spiritual path.
rows.anchor: was bodily as well as spiritual and considers it a special miracle granted to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A well-known hadith calls canonical prayer the believers’ ascension, while mystical literature treats the Prophet’s journey as a prototype for spiritual encounter with God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Night Journey became a major theme in Islamic mystical literature, miniature painting, and poetry; its accounts may have influenced Dante’s Divine Comedy through descriptions of the heavens reaching the Latin West.
rows.anchor: Elements of the account of the Prophet’s Night Journey may have even influenced accounts of mystical journeying in other traditions, such as Dante’s Divine Comedy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jerusalem is Islam’s third holiest site because of the Night Journey and Ascension; it was the first qiblah until prayer direction changed to Makkah in 2/624 after 2:143–44.
rows.anchor: The direction of prayer was changed from Jerusalem to Makkah in the year 2/624, after the revelation of 2:143–44

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse briefly alludes to the horizontal isrāʾ from Makkah to Jerusalem; 53:1–18 alludes to the vertical miʿrāj through the heavens to the Divine Throne and encounter with God.
rows.anchor: The present verse is considered to refer to the first, “horizontal,” part of the journey, from Makkah to Jerusalem

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “His servant” means Muhammad; the Farthest Mosque denotes the ancient Temple site in Jerusalem, now the Dome of the Rock precinct, where the Prophet ascended.
rows.anchor: His servant is a reference to Muhammad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because asrā already means travel by night, laylan emphasizes that the otherwise month-long Makkah–Jerusalem journey and return occurred in one night.
rows.anchor: The verb asrā by itself means to travel at night

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most identify the Sacred Mosque with the Kaʿbah sanctuary itself; some broaden it to Makkah’s environs, while hadith describing Gabriel rousing Muhammad in the sanctuary supports the literal reading.
rows.anchor: the literal reading of the verse indicates that he left from the Sacred Mosque itself

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The Farthest Mosque is so named because it was the farthest sacred site the Prophet visited and the farthest place where he prayed, although he likely traveled farther to Damascus before prophethood.
rows.anchor: because it was the farthest sacred place visited by the Prophet and the farthest place in which he prayed during his lifetime

rows.speaker: some reports
rows.claim: The blessed precincts mean Jerusalem and its environs, the Biblical land of Canaan; reports explain the blessing as fertile land and abundant crops.
rows.anchor: Some reports indicate that the blessedness of the land referred to its fertility and its abundant fruits and crops

rows.speaker: other reports
rows.claim: Other reports understand Jerusalem’s blessing as worldly and spiritual bounty because many prophets worshipped there or received revelation there.
rows.anchor: others indicate that it was blessed with both worldly and spiritual bounty, since many prophets had worshipped or received revelation there

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs shown to the Prophet can include the miraculous journey and its reported visions and encounters with earlier prophets, angels, and God.
rows.anchor: Our signs may include the miraculous journey itself as well as the visions and encounters with past prophets, angels, and God Himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book given to Moses is the Torah.
rows.anchor: The Book given to Moses is the Torah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to take no guardian besides God recalls Quranic reminders that no protector exists other than God.
rows.anchor: The command to the Israelites, Take no guardian apart from Me, is similar to reminders throughout the Quran that one has no protector other than God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The progeny of those whom We carried with Noah” further describes the Children of Israel.
rows.anchor: The progeny of those whom We carried with Noah is an additional description of the Children of Israel in v. 2.

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most understand God’s decree in the Book as God informing Israel in the Torah of the future events described.
rows.anchor: is understood by most to mean that God informed the Israelites in the Torah of the events alluded to in this verse

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some understand the decree as recording the future events in the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: Some, however, understand this to mean that God decreed these future events in the Preserved Tablet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here, Israel’s two corruptions mean serious deviations from Torah commands; some commentators connect them with crises such as killing prophets.
rows.anchor: the Israelites will work corruption upon the earth twice is understood to refer to times of serious deviation from the commands of the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two corruptions may allude to Jerusalem Temple destructions in 586 BCE and 70 CE, or to the falls of Israel in 722 BCE and Judah in 586 BCE.
rows.anchor: the present verse may be an allusion to the two times when the Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Classical commentators mention people and events from these periods but show chronological confusion and do not map the two corruptions neatly onto either historical sequence.
rows.anchor: there is significant chronological confusion in the reports. The commentators thus do not present these two instances of corruption and destruction as directly or schematically fitting

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Although “ascend to great height” sounds positive, commentators interpret it as tyranny, rebellion against God, or great arrogance toward Him.
rows.anchor: the commentators understand it to mean that the Israelites had become tyrants

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Commentators identify the leader sent against Israel as Goliath, Sennacherib, or Nebuchadnezzar.
rows.anchor: some identify the leader of the servants of Ours whom God sent against the Israelites as Goliath, Sennacherib, or Nebudchadnezzar

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Other commentators say the invaders’ identity is unimportant; their defeat of Israel exemplifies collective moral and spiritual failure.
rows.anchor: Some commentators, however, suggest that the identity of those sent against the Israelites is not significant; what is important is the concept that such a fate befell the Israelites at times of collective moral and spiritual failing

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Ravaging the dwellings includes plundering homes and wealth, destroying sacred objects, desecrating the Temple, burning Torah scrolls, killing readers, and taking survivors captive.
rows.anchor: referring to the plundering of homes and wealth and the destruction of sacred objects, including the desecration of the Temple, the burning of the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fulfilled promise is a fate decreed by God and therefore unavoidable.
rows.anchor: it was a fate decreed by God that could not be avoided

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God restored Israel’s fortunes after they repented of the corruption and arrogance in verse 4.
rows.anchor: God gave the Israelites a turn against them, after they had repented of the corruption and arrogance mentioned in v. 4

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some connect Israel’s reversal with Goliath’s killing; more commonly it means Babylon’s defeat, liberation, return to Jerusalem’s surroundings, and the rise of new prophets.
rows.anchor: Some consider this change of fortune to refer to the killing of Goliath or, more commonly, to the defeat of Babylon

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children signify earthly prosperity, while being greater in number means population growth.
rows.anchor: wealth and children are two common signifiers of earthly good fortune in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The consequences of virtue and evil fall on their agents; the Quran repeats this principle, and 55:60 asks whether goodness receives any reward but goodness.
rows.anchor: The idea that the consequences of moral or immoral actions ultimately devolve upon those who commit them is conveyed in various ways throughout the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other promise is the second attack on Israel; some link it to Herod’s execution of John the Baptist and the Roman occupation and Temple’s second destruction.
rows.anchor: Some reports connect this second set of events with the Jewish king Herod’s execution of John the Baptist

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says identifying the precise Israelite historical events is unnecessary for interpreting the passage’s ultimate meaning.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī, who suggests that interpreting the ultimate meaning of this passage should not be dependent upon knowing the specific details of Israelite history

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some anachronistically associate the second Temple destruction with Nebuchadnezzar, despite the Roman destruction and chronological mismatch.
rows.anchor: the destruction mentioned in this verse is associated by some commentators, anachronistically, with Nebuchadnezzar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making faces wretched means grief and distress will become visible; the face symbolizes the soul in the Quran, including in depictions of judgment and Hell.
rows.anchor: meaning that the grief and distress that will befall the Israelites will show on their faces

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may remove Israel’s adversity if they repent; some commentators take “may have mercy” to mean He certainly did or will.
rows.anchor: The Lord may have mercy upon the Israelites and remove the adversity visited upon them if they repent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Israel returns to corruption, God will punish them again; some see 7:167 as implying this pattern lasts until Resurrection.
rows.anchor: if they again revert to corruption, God will also revert, meaning that He will punish them again

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell is an inescapable prison unlike earthly punishment; ḥaṣīr may also mean mat or cushion, ironically portraying Hell as the disbelievers’ resting place.
rows.anchor: the punishments of Hell are inescapable and surround the condemned on every side like a prison

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: “That which is most upright” can refer to truth or religion; the grammatically feminine pronoun leads others to read it as the straight path or upright community or creed.
rows.anchor: That the Quran guides toward that which is most upright can mean that it guides to the truth or to religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “great reward” promised to believers is the paradisal Garden.
rows.anchor: The great reward is a reference to the paradisal Garden

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: People may ignorantly pray for what seems beneficial but will actually harm them, or in anger curse themselves, family, or property; answering such prayers would destroy humanity.
rows.anchor: people pray in ignorance for what seems beneficial to them but will only bring them harm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human haste appears in rushing toward disbelief, sin, and enmity, seeking evil before good, and demanding warned-of punishments; 21:37 calls haste intrinsic to humanity.
rows.anchor: people hasten unto disbelief (5:41) and to sin and enmity (5:62)

rows.speaker: a report
rows.claim: A report says Adam impatiently tried to stand before the Spirit had reached his feet as life entered his body from his head downward.
rows.anchor: when God breathed His Spirit into Adam, He started from the head, and as the Spirit flowed downward

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day are signs of divine power and beneficence: night allows repose, while daylight enables seeking bounty, as many Quranic passages note.
rows.anchor: These are both signs of God’s Power and Beneficence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their regular alternation lets people count years and reckon time through the cycles of sun and moon.
rows.anchor: The regular alternation between day and night also allows people to know the number of years and “reckon” time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Expounded everything in detail” means God has explained it clearly in the Quran; His signs and Book are similarly described as expounded.
rows.anchor: That God has expounded all things in detail means that He has explained them clearly (Ṭ) in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāʾirah (“omen”) derives from the root for birds because early Arabs and other premodern societies treated birds’ behavior as signs of fortune or consequences.
rows.anchor: since the early Arabs, like certain other premodern societies, considered the movement and behavior of birds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omen fastened on the neck depicts foreknown destiny as sealed; the neck also bears tokens of honor or shame such as necklaces, chains, and collars.
rows.anchor: That God has fastened a human being’s omen upon his neck is an image used to convey the idea that God has foreknowledge of a human being’s ultimate destiny

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators identify the omen with a person’s deeds, which portend bliss or misery in the Hereafter, and also with that individual’s Divine Decree (qadar).
rows.anchor: Many commentators consider the omen upon one’s neck to represent one’s deeds in life, which, like an omen, portend either bliss or wretchedness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Traditions say each person is divinely apportioned a lifespan, provision, offspring, and status in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: all human beings are born with a Divinely apportioned life span, material provision, and number of offspring

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse and traditions can support predestination, but can instead indicate God’s foreknowledge of eventual moral choices and fate; some read the omen as moral responsibility (taklīf) under divine law.
rows.anchor: Both these traditions and the present verse can be read in a predestinarian vein to indicate that all moral destiny is foreordained

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The open book is the record of one’s deeds, familiar to the person and God; hidden earthly deeds and consequences become manifest in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: That an individual’s book is wide open indicates that its contents are well known to the individual as well as to God

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators say two angels assigned to each person record good and evil deeds.
rows.anchor: The recording of deeds is often ascribed to two angels assigned to every individual, one recording good deeds and the other evil deeds

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī metaphorically pictures each deed as a drop leaving an impression on the soul’s rock; repeated habits help inscribe a person’s destiny.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī, however, describes the spiritual reality of this recording metaphorically, suggesting that every deed one commits in life is like a drop of water

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God, perhaps speaking through angels, commands each person to read the record and thereby judge whether their own deeds merit Garden or Fire.
rows.anchor: who issues the command in v. 14, Read your book!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although divine mercy remains beyond calculation and inspires hope, people are saved or condemned through their actions; God does not wrong them, they wrong themselves.
rows.anchor: human beings are saved or condemned through their own actions. For this reason, the Quran repeatedly states that God does not wrong people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book can be one’s soul inscribed with deeds, and the Quran elsewhere depicts one’s limbs testifying against one at Judgment.
rows.anchor: the Quran offers elsewhere the powerful image of one’s own limbs testifying against one on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some describe the book as the person themself, with tongue as pen, saliva as ink, limbs as paper, and memory as the dictated record.
rows.anchor: Your tongue is its pen, your saliva is its ink, and your limbs are the paper upon which it is written

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance and misguidance bring consequences to the person; the verse also reiterates that no one bears another’s sin, though misleaders may bear an added burden.
rows.anchor: This verse brings together three themes commonly invoked throughout the Quran, including the related ideas that the consequences of one’s moral actions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not punish a people before warning them by sending a messenger; other verses state the same principle.
rows.anchor: That God does not punish a people without warning, identified here specifically with His sending a messenger, is mentioned elsewhere

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Privileged leaders and high-status people often resist prophets’ warnings and disbelieve, as illustrated throughout the Quran.
rows.anchor: it is often the privileged members of a community—its leaders and those who enjoy high social status—who are most resistant to the warnings of the prophets

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators understand God’s command to the luxurious as a command to believe and obey, which they disobey by committing iniquity.
rows.anchor: We command those who live a life of luxury is understood by most commentators to mean that God commands such people to belief and obedience

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reads “when We desire to destroy” as when the known destruction approaches; God commands the privileged, knowing they will disobey.
rows.anchor: when We desire to destroy a town means when the time draws near for the destruction of a town whose fate is already known to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Privilege makes disobedience less excusable because of abundant blessings, even if worldly attractions may tempt the privileged more strongly.
rows.anchor: The disobedience and disbelief of people of privilege is in some ways the least excusable because of the many blessings they have been given

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the command to commit iniquity is metaphorical: giving means and power to disobey is as if commanding it, since God does not command indecency.
rows.anchor: al-Zamakhsharī and others point out, the Quran clearly states that God does not command indecency

rows.speaker: some readers
rows.claim: Some read amarnā as ammarnā, meaning God places the luxurious in positions of authority.
rows.anchor: Some have read the verbal phrase amarnā, We command, as ammarnā, meaning that God places those who live a life of luxury in positions of authority

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Word coming due means respite has expired and threatened punishment is imminent; the town’s destruction uproots it completely.
rows.anchor: That the Word comes due for a town or a people indicates that their period of respite has elapsed and the threatened Divine Punishment is imminent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In sacred history Noah begins the succession of prophets whose peoples were destroyed for rejecting repentance and tawḥīd; the Quran repeatedly presents destroyed nations as signs to heed.
rows.anchor: Noah is the first in a series of prophets whose peoples were destroyed for rejecting the message of repentance and tawḥīd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those seeking only worldly goods while denying or despairing of the Hereafter may receive what they want here, subject to God’s will, and then face Hell.
rows.anchor: God may hasten for them precisely what they desire; that is, He may grant them worldly goods in the here and now, but with the caveat whatsoever We will for whomsoever We desire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God appreciates sincere believers’ efforts for the Hereafter; His appreciation, literally thankfulness, is their reward there.
rows.anchor: God’s appreciation (lit. “thankfulness”) for their deeds is the reward He grants them in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse grounds judging deeds by intentions: reward requires intending good, earnestly attempting it, and being a believer, without requiring completion or success.
rows.anchor: This verse is an important basis for the Islamic doctrine that deeds are judged according to their intentions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those desiring the ephemeral may include people performing apparently pious acts hypocritically or only for worldly gain.
rows.anchor: Those who desire the ephemeral in v. 18 may include not only those whose worldly desires lead them to outwardly sinful behavior

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet’s hadith says deeds are according to intentions, illustrated by emigrants whose reward depends on whether they emigrated for God or worldly benefit such as marriage.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said in a famous ḥadīth, “Deeds are only according to intentions, and verily each shall have what he intended

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God provides both the worldly-minded and Hereafter-seeking because His earthly gift is not restricted to either group.
rows.anchor: God aids both those who desire the ephemeral (v. 18) and whosoever desires the Hereafter (v. 19), for God’s Gift, meaning earthly provision, is not confined

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some understand the greater worldly favor of Hereafter-seekers as sound judgment, a gift more valuable than ephemeral goods.
rows.anchor: may indicate that whosoever desires the Hereafter have been given the greater gift, namely, sound judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, God may distribute worldly provision in different degrees among believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: It might also simply indicate that God gives and withholds provision in different degrees among both believers and disbelievers

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī links unequal worldly livelihoods and rank to service and testing, citing 43:32 and 6:165; Hereafter distinctions between Garden and Fire are greater and clearer.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī observes that the Divine purpose behind such differences in earthly provision is elucidated in 43:32

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse repeats the Quranic warning against worshipping partners, equals, or other gods alongside God.
rows.anchor: repeated Quranic warnings against “setting up”partners (e.g., 3:151; 4:48; 13:16)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to worship God alone paired with kindness to parents recurs in several Quranic passages.
rows.anchor: For other verses in which the imperative to worship God is paired with a command to be good to parents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s decree to worship Him alone can mean a command, or that ultimately all things worship Him, as 13:15 and 17:44 say.
rows.anchor: That the Lord decrees that you worship none but Him can mean that He commands it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse asks children to tolerate elderly parents’ needs as their parents once patiently cared for them; uff can express complaint or annoyance.
rows.anchor: the implication here is that one should be tolerant and patient with parents and their needs and dependencies, just as they were patient with one as a child

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some understand uff as something filthy or soiling, addressing irritation at assisting elderly parents with personal hygiene.
rows.anchor: some thus suggest that the verse is addressing the irritation a son or daughter might feel in having to assist elderly parents with personal hygiene

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on saying uff also discourages any ugly, harsh, or dismissive expression; tanharhumā can mean rebuffing or angrily turning away.
rows.anchor: The prohibition against saying Uff! to one’s parents may also be meant to discourage the use of any kind of ugly, harsh, or dismissive expression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lowering the wing of humility means treating parents with abundant mercy, affection, and humility; a child’s mercy and prayer repay their early care.
rows.anchor: To lower . . . the wing of humility out of mercy expresses the abundance of mercy, affection, and humility with which children should treat their parents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if parents disbelieve, children should pray for God’s mercy upon them, particularly asking for their guidance.
rows.anchor: even if one’s parents are disbelievers, one should still pray for God’s Mercy upon them, asking particularly that He give them guidance

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī cites a hadith that God’s contentment follows parental contentment and His anger follows their anger.
rows.anchor: al-Zamakhsharī cites the ḥadīth:“The Contentment of God lies in the contentment of parents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s knowledge of what is in souls is echoed by verses saying He knows what lies in breasts and hearts.
rows.anchor: That God knows what is in souls is also mentioned in 2:234 and 11:31. Similarly, He is said to know what lies within breasts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The duty to give kin, the indigent, and travelers their due is linked to similar charity commands, including 30:38 and 59:7.
rows.anchor: For a very similar verse, see 30:38; see also 2:83, 177, 215; 4:36

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Giving kin their right can mean sustaining family relations and visiting relatives often, a major principle of Islamic ethics.
rows.anchor: To give unto the kinsman his right may mean to maintain good relations with one’s kin and to visit them often

rows.speaker: ʿAlī Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn
rows.claim: A report from ʿAlī Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn identifies the kinsman as Muhammad’s family, entitled to their allotted share of bounties and spoils because ordinary charity was forbidden to them.
rows.anchor: A report attributed to ʿAlī Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn (d. 92/711), the pious great-grandson of the Prophet and the fourth Shiite Imam, understands kinsman

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Giving the traveler his due can mean supplying food or accommodation.
rows.anchor: To give unto . . . the traveler may mean to provide travelers with food or accommodation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Charity must not be excessive, wasteful for pride or reputation, or diverted from those with a moral claim; avoid both prodigality and miserliness.
rows.anchor: one should not squander such charity wastefully by being excessive in one’s giving

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The wasteful are Satan’s brethren in the sense that they are his friends and supporters.
rows.anchor: Those who are wasteful are the brethren of satans, meaning that they are their friends and supporters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although verses 28–30 address the Prophet, their injunctions apply to all believers; turning away here means being unable to fulfill a request for charity.
rows.anchor: Vv. 28–30 are addressed to the Prophet, but the injunctions they contain apply to all believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking mercy may describe temporary poverty: the Prophet hopes and trusts God will eventually provide what he needs.
rows.anchor: to call poverty a state of seeking a mercy from God suggests both the temporary nature of the Prophet’s state of need and his hope and trust

rows.speaker: a report
rows.claim: One report says that when unable to provide charity, the Prophet stayed silent while waiting for provision rather than refuse the request.
rows.anchor: It is reported that when the Prophet was asked for charity that he could not provide, he would remain silent while the provision was not available

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should instead explain gently that he lacks means now and encourage petitioners with a promise of God’s coming provision.
rows.anchor: but encouraging and promising them that provision from God shall come (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Another reading is “speak for them gentle words,” meaning pray for God to grant the petitioners’ needs.
rows.anchor: indicating that the Prophet should supplicate God on their behalf to grant them the needed provision

rows.speaker: an alternate interpretation
rows.claim: An alternate occasion says the verse followed the Prophet refusing charity to people he knew would use it for corruption; he sought God’s mercy by preventing it.
rows.anchor: An alternate interpretation explains that this verse was revealed after the Prophet refused to grant the requested charity to a group of people whom he knew would use the funds to engage in corruption

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God controls all earthly provision, and a well-known Prophetic hadith includes provision among what God decrees for each person.
rows.anchor: indicates that God controls all earthly provision, an idea also found in a well-known ḥadīth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yabsuṭu shares a root with the Divine Name al-Bāsiṭ (“the Open-Handed”), a name absent from the Quran; divine open-handedness appears in 5:64.
rows.anchor: Outspreads translates yabsuṭu, and this action, attributed to God here and elsewhere, is derived from the same root as the Divine Name al-Bāsiṭ
